On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. leader
of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) inquired when the annual report of the Canadian National Railways would be available. I find that the auditors have completed their work. The report is now in the hands of the printers, and I expect to lay it on the table of the house before the Easter adjournment.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Quebec-harbours and rivers generally- repairs and improvements, $100,000.
How much was spent under this head last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The amount spent last year was

Item agreed to.
lie Perrot-dredging, $8,000.

Where is He
Perrot, and is this work that has to be done every year, or is this a contract for some specific work?

lie Perrot is a post village in Vaudreuil county, about six miles from Ste. Anne de Bellevue, on the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. This is a revote, which is required to complete the contract which was entered into last year.

Item agreed to.
Lake St. Louis-dredging, $47,000.
Does this department do all the dredging in lake St. Louis, or is some of it done by the Marine and Fisheries department?
That department does no dredging above Montreal.
Will this amount complete the work?
It will complete the contract that has been entered into. Of course, this is a place where dredging has to be done pretty constantly.

Item agreed to.
Little Montreal river-dredging-the provincial government to contribute a like amount, $14,000.
I notice that the cost is divided with the provincial government. Why is that?

A contract was awarded in December, 1928, to G. Lorrain by the county of Napierville, amounting to $30,487, upon the understanding that the Dominion government and provincial government would each pay half the cost of each progress estimate up to a total of $30,000, the supervision to be made by the federal engineer's office. Order in council, dated February 6, 1929, gave authority to -confirm the above arrangement, and for the Dominion government to pay one-half of the progress estimates to be submitted, such payments to be made as the work proceeded, and not to exceed the amount of the contribution voted, $15,000. Since that time, however, during the progress of the work, it was found that the material encountered was much harder than anticipated, and the contractor, after removing some of this at considerable

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
difficulty by blasting, had to discontinue the work on November 15, 1929. The contractor claims that he should be paid for this material at rock prices, $2.25 per yard, as contained in the contract, and the matter is being dealt with by negotiations between this department, the provincial Department of Agriculture, and the county. I might say that this is carrying out work which was started in 1928, but on account of delays, due to the different governments interested, we have only made such progress as I have stated.
What differentiates this work from many other items where the provincial government is interested? Why does not the provincial government pay half of the other items?

It is one of those matters where it is claimed that the Dominion government should contribute. This is similar to Norton's creek and some other cases where both governments have been doing the work for a number of years.
The reference to Norton's creek is rather unfortunate, as I understand that was really for the purpose of drainage. Is this item the same sort of thing; is it really a drainage scheme?
I would not say that it is a drainage scheme, but it is not dissimilar to Norton's creek.
What is the character of the work that is actually being done? The minister has not yet given a definite reply.
It is dredging in the Little Montreal river.
Why are the two governments interested? It is rather unusual, is it not?
It is both a dredging and a drainage proposition, and each government claims it should be done by the other. So a compromise arrangement was arrived at under which each contributes to the cost.
After the dredging is done will the channel be of any use for boats?
Only for very small boats.
How large?
Row boats.
Much larger than that.

Item agreed to.
Manicouagan river-wharf-one-third of cost to be contributed jointly by the Ontario Paper Co., Ltd., and the Anglo Canadian Pulp and Paper Co., $275,000.
This appears to be an old acquaintance. Would the minister be good enough to give us some information in regard to it?

Yes. This amount is required to cover the government's share of the completion of the contract entered into in September, 1929, with Messrs. Farley & Grant and Cummins & Robinson for the construction of a wharf, 1,900 feet long, the first 1,000 feet to be formed of a stone embankment and the next 900 feet of cribwork. This wharf is being built in connection with the construction of pulp and paper mills and power development near the mouth of the Manicouagan river by the Ontario Paper Co. Ltd., and the Anglo Canadian Pulp and Paper Co., these two companies having agreed to contribute one-third of the total cost of the work.
One-third each, or one-third between them?
One-third between the two.
What is the estimated total cost?
The chief engineer's estimate for the total work to be done was $417,450. The amount of the contract is $474,774.
How much has been spent already?
What constituency is it in?
Charlevoix-Saguenay.

Will this remain the
property of the Dominion government?
Yes.
Will there be any charges for its use by the companies?
No.
Will any person have the right to use the wharf?

Yes, it is a public wharf; everybody will have the right to use it. These two companies are making large expenditures in the vicinity at the present time, and the reason they are contributing is that they will be more directly interested than the general public
1038	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
Will the chief whip of the Liberal party (Mr. Casgrain) give us the particulars of this work? He will probably know more about it than the Minister of Public Works.
I doubt it very much.
I do not doubt it at all. I understand this is in the constituency of the chief Liberal whip. Perhaps he will be able to explain to the house fully what the expenditure is for.

This is a development
similar to others that have been carried on in certain parts of Quebec and also in other provinces. Manicouagan is situated about 250 miles below the city of Quebec. The Anglo-Canadian Pulp and Paper Company and the Ontario Paper Company, Limited, have obtained from the provincial government a lease of all the timber limits in the watershed east of the Manicouagan river, the largest timber limits in the province on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. The two companies have an agreement with the provincial government, a copy of which was deposited with the Department of Public Works, under which the companies covenant with the provincial government to establish pulp mills at Manicouagan and have them in operation by 1931. The provincial government is assisting the two companies to develop the town by providing a road from the site to the wharf. During the course of this summer or early next year the projected town will have, it is estimated, a population of 4,000 or 5,000 people. It is claimed that the new municipality will be a source of revenue both to the provincial and federal governments because the pulp mills will give employment to a large number of people living in the vicinity. I may say that the provincial government has also helped the Anglo-Canadian Pulp and Paper Company to develop a place called Clark City on the north shore of the St. Lawrence very much along the same lines, and in that instance years ago, the federal government, under another administration, paid the whole cost of the wharf. The Ontario Paper Company, Limited, owns and operates timber limits at other places along the north shore, one in Shelter Bay and the other at Franklin. These two are the largest and most reliable companies engaged in the wood and paper industry in the province of Quebec.

I congratulate the hon.
member on how much he knows with respect to this item. He has given us a great deal more information than the Minister of Public Works did.
He took longer.

Of course the minister was interested in taking a shorter time. Will the chief whip of the liberal party inform us if the Clarks interested in Clark City are the same gentlemen who run steam boats down the north shore of the St. Lawrence?

The man who founded
Clark City about twenty-five or thirty years ago was the uncle of the men who operate the steamship company and who own the Gidf of St. Lawrence Paper Company, Limited. The company at Clark City and the Anglo-Canadian Pulp and Paper Company, I may say, are financed by English capital furnished by the Rothermere interests in England, who own one of the largest newspaper concerns in the old country.

Are the Clarks who run
the steamship line interested in this?

No, it is a different
company.
But are they interested in this?
I do not think so.
But both gave their name to the city and the steamship company. I think the chief whip has made a very good defence of the item for the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain).
"Defence" is a good word.

Are there any
operations going on there at present; are they making paper now?

At the present time these people cannot start to operate and cannot fulfil their contract with the provincial government, and no work can be carried on in that district until this wharf is built. In the course of a few months or a year there will be a town located there, but at present it is a wilderness with rocks, cliffs, mountains, hills and forest. Last summer the townsite was cleared up and laid out by a company under the control of these two companies; much of that work has been done, and I remember being told by some of the officers of these two companies that during last summer between 300 and 400 people ware employed on this work.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec

How many men do they
expect to employ in the paper mill, and when do they expect to turn out paper?

I cannot very well give that information but it must be in the hands of the minister, because when these people applied for this work I think they deposited with the minister a copy of the contract with the provincial government. The provincial government called upon these companies to start work within a given period, and they will turn out the finished product in the province of Quebec.
Taking into consideration the present condition of the paper trade does not my hon. friend think it would be just as well if this company did not start work too soon?

I believe that question
was discussed last year. Hon. members will recall that a few years ago, I think in 1927, an amount of $100,000 was placed in the estimates in order to start the work that year, but the following year that item was dropped because at that time there seemed to be some unsettlement in the pulp and paper business. Since then pressure has been brought to bear on these two companies to proceed with the work, and those interested in the pulp and paper industry are satisfied that work may be started now, because it is hoped that in the very near future the situation to which my hon. friend has referred will be adjusted.

It was only last year, I think, that a similar amount was in the estimates for another paper concern down in Anticosti, in this same constituency. This seems to be a pretty large amount for this government to be giving a private concern. We might build pulp mills all over the country if we could get the government to contribute $200,000, $300,000 or $400,000 in order to start things going. It is almost impossible for us in the maritime provinces to get grants in order to carry on our general business and to repair the breakwaters and piers which we aleady have, but it is nothing for the province of Quebec to get S275,000 or S300.000 for the assistance of some pulp mill. If this pulp mill has received such wonderful concessions from the provincial government of Quebec, it seems to me it should be in a position to build its own wharf.
Will this be a company town, in the ordinary sense of the word?

No, it is going to be a
public town and is to be called Taschereau. It will be built and operated under the act which regulates such townships and municipalities in the province of Quebec.

Now I have the secret of
the grants and concessions that have been made by the Quebec provincial government. These Americans came to the government and said, "We want this and that, and we will give the name of the Premier to the town we intend to build." So then the Premier said, "Carried; you may have it." I think these people showed great ability in securing what they requested; they were very keen and very astute in getting these privileges from the province of Quebec. I have not a word of criticism for the chief whip of the Liberal party, nor do I suggest that he should not get a substantial amount of money for these improvements.
I do not get it personally; my people will enjoy the privileges.

I never thought my hon.
friend was to do the dredging himself, but I am sure it will be for the benefit of his constituents. I am not so narrow minded as to ask these people to change the name of the town, but that gives me the answer to the whole problem. I should not have spoken on this item at all if some mention had not been made of grants by the provincial government. I think we should be very careful, not in the amounts which are asked for by my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay, but in connection with these contracts which are entered into by the Quebec government with foreigners. It seems to me that when a foreigner comes to the Quebec government for a grant he has a greater chance of getting it than a native son of Canada would have. That is why I bring this matter to the attention of the committee. I am not criticizing the item; I think my hon. friend has done right in looking after his constituents and trying to improve conditions in his constituency, but I think in future the depai-tment should be very careful in any assistance it may give to companies having contracts with the Quebec government.
Am I correct in my understanding that the contract was completed in 1927?
No.
I thought the minister gave the date as 1927.

No, 1929.
1040	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec

At page 36 of the estimates for 1929, I find the sum of SI00,000 for this purpose. Then I turn to the estimates for the following year and find that for some reason the item disappeared entirely. Then when I turn to the estimates for this year I find that the item reappears, together with a reference to a vote in 1929-30. I suppose that must have come out of the general appropriation. As far as I can tell from the estimates which I have here the vote first appeared at page 36 of the items for 1929.
No, I think my hon. friend is wrong about the year. Last year would be 1929; we call these the 1930 estimates.

I may be wrong as to when it first appeared, but I think I am right with respect to the year I stated. I then find that in the following year this item is not in the estimates at all, but in the estimates for this year we find a revote of $50,000, which seems to indicate that they must have had some money from somewhere.
It was in the supplementary estimates of last year. It was in the estimates of 1927 but was dropped the following year, and was only placed in the supplementary estimates at the end of last session.

Do I understand that a contract was entered into between the Public Works department and some contractor and that, pursuant to the contract, contributions were to be made by these two companies, or was the contract between two other parties with contributions from the Department of Public Works? No matter how the contract was made I should like to find out from the minister to what exent the two companies in question have put up cash in connection with the work, up to the present time.

I think perhaps what
causes confusion is the practice of referring to the estimates of the year before last as the 1929 estimates. We usually refer to the estimates now under consideration as those for 1930; last year's estimates were for 1929 and those of the previous year were the 1928 estimates. The item appeared in the estimates of 1928.

In order to make it clear, I am merely taking the year which appears upon the estimates themselves. The estimates which I am calling the 1929 estimates are for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929. Then we have the estimates for 1930', and I have already said that nothing appeared in the main estimates for that year.

As has been explained by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken, this item first appeared in the estimates for 192728. Since there was a slowing up in the business the work was not proceeded with and the item was dropped from the main estimates of 1928-29, but an item was placed in the supplementary estimates. That was the item amounting to $100,000. The contract was only to be entered into by the Department of Public Works upon the assurance that the work which was contemplated, which was a very large work, would go on. When the department became satisfied of that fact, they took bonds from the companies which are to contribute as a guarantee of payment, and then let the contract for the work. In answer to the hon. member who asked with regard to the amount of freight which would be handled on this wharf, I think it would be interesting for the house to know that the incoming freight is estimated as follows:
Material for production of 19,000 tons sulphite and ground wood pulp, including sulphur, coal, limestone, stores, repairs, et cetera, to the value of 81,000,000.
Provisions, materials, tools, and equipment for cutting and preparing 300,000 cords of wood, to the value of $2,200,000.
Provisions and general supplies for a population estimated to be from 10,000 to 15,000' when operations have commenced, to the value of $1,250,000. That makes a total of $4,450,000 for the incoming freight.
The combined total of the incoming and outgoing freight is estimated to be valued at $9,080,000. It should be borne in mind that these estimates are made upon the present plans, but both companies have increased production in mind as soon as other plans have been consummated. Of course, the condition of the industry since this item was first inserted in the estimates has not been as favourable as present prospects indicate.

What cash contribution has
been made by these companies? These estimates are very interesting, and I do not want to be considered as criticizing this item-I do not know enough about it either to approve of or criticize it-but it is asked that a quarter of a million dollars be voted and we should have very complete information. I think the minister should give us some information as to what these companies are to do, and what they have done. His information as to the probable business is all very interesting and may be quite true, but I remember well some information which was given to us regarding Belle River. It was contended that wonderful

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
business would ensue at that point, but the whole thing has been discarded and the money was thrown away and wasted. I do not say that this vote will be wasted but perhaps we have been taught a lesson, and we should be a little careful after voting $130,000 in the other instance.

The reason I did not go
into the details which I have here, and which cover many pages, was because the whole matter had been discussed in the house when the estimate was first inserted. As my hon. friend has said, there is a contract, entered into with the Quebec government by which the companies agreed to make these expenditures and to employ a certain number of hands.
That is between the companies and the Quebec government?

Between the companies
' and the Quebec government. That contract has been deposited with the Dominion government and bonds have been taken from the companies to guarantee the construction of the wharf. The hon. member for Cumberland wondered why it was done in this way, but I may say that the same policy has been adopted before.

When was I shifted to
Cumberland?

I should have said the
hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short); it would be a bad thing for Digby to have my hon. friend shifted to any other part of the province. This same arrangement was made in the Brooklyn case, where the Mersey Paper Company is located and I think the same procedure was followed with the Thunder bay and the Powell river cases.

As I understand it, the contract referred to would be one between the companies and the province of Quebec and would have to do with the concessions the companies were getting from that province, the companies in turn having to do certain things. The contract we are dealing with is the one between the Department of Public Works and this company, and I would like to know something about what these companies have undertaken. If they have agreed to pay one-third of the cost, have they paid it? It is all very well to promise these things when prospects are bright, but apparently they have not been so good lately. I am prompted by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) to ask the kind of bonds given by the company, are they guaranteed bonds or bonds
of the respective companies? I am very anxious to find out how much cash has been put up by these companies in connection with this contract, for which we are asked to vote such a large sum of money.
There has been no cash put up; they put up bonds of a guarantee company.
For the payment of their share of the costs?
Yes.
How much cash has the department paid out already on these contracts?
The total is $75,000.
If that is so, then we should have got $25,000 from the two companies. Why has that not been paid? What effort has been made by the. department to collect, and why have they not been successful?

I cannot tell my hon. friend the amount which has been paid, but the practice is to render a bill every month for their respective shares. Where the security is so large as it is in the present case, we do not worry particularly as to whether it is paid right on the day.

If the income tax is not paid right on the day we incur an immediate penalty, and in this particular instance, if the department is entitled to it, I do not see why it should not try to get it. Perhaps the minister could tell us how many accounts have been sent out.
I have not those details here. In a contract of over a quarter of a million dollars, the question of $75,000 is a very small part of the contract.
It is much easier to pay when it is so small.
Much easier to pay, but a smaller risk when the security is so large.
Is the department receiving interest?
I would not say that.

Why not? The interest on $25,000 is a respectable amount. I was amazed at the figures given by the minister in connection with the expected traffic. They remind me of the prospectuses which are got out by some companies when they are floating: these pulp mills, and I recall one in particular down in my own province.

That would be a good one,. I would think.
1042	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec

The facts were just as rosy as those presented by the minister, but unfortunately the wheels in the mill never turned, and this case may prove to be similar. We had an expenditure in 192S of $300,000 at Ellis Bay, which is in the same constituency.
That was reduced to

In 1927-28 they spent $150,000, and $300,000 was spent in 1928-29. No wonder there are so many pulp mills in the province of Quebec. When they know they can come to this government and obtain grants such as this I can quite understand why so many mills are built in that province. I wonder when this sort of thing is going to stop. Probably there will be another one next year, because the hon. member who represents that constituency tells us that it is proposed to build two more towns down there.
The development work in those cases is being done by the companies themselves.

This seems to be a rather remarkable wharf, because judging from the information given by the minister it will be about a third of a mile long. Has anything been done by the promoters referred to beyond putting out the prospectus, or has the whole thing floated in on the dew? How did they get any plant there if the deep water end of a wharf yet to be built is 1,900 feet iway from the shore?

I understand the work has seen proceeded with. There were 300 men working there all last year. The power development has been completed and the company has, I understand, made very substantial progress which makes it necessary that the wharf should be in shape for use this year.
Does that mean they will be producing paper this year?

No, but it is necessary to have the wharf because such an immense amount of shipping is required in connection with the construction. This is a $10,000,000 construction and they cannot get the materials, machinery and that sort of thing in there without a wharf.

Is any time limit set
when the mill will be completed and in operation?
I believe it is calculated it will be producing in 1932.
Is there any railway communication with this point?
No.

Then I gather there cannot have been any machinery actually delivered on the site or on the plant. The wharf is not completed. There is no railway. The outer end of the wharf is 1,900 feet from the shore. It is quite evdent to any hon. member who considers the situation that there can be no machinery there. There has been no development except on paper. Is that not correct?
I do not wonder at my hon. friend coming to that conclusion because that is just what I have told him, namely, that they cannot get the machinery in until the wharf is constructed.

Has the minister made any inquiry as to the financial standing of the companies themselves? What cash has been put up? They first go and get a concession from the province of Quebec. The next thing is the flotation of the company and the sale of bonds. When was the first demand for their share of the cost made upon the companies and how many times has that demand been made since without anything being paid up to date?
These are two companies: the Ontario Paper Company Limited and the Anglo Canadian Pulp and Paper Company.
That means nothing in itself

They already have large mills, one at Thorold and the other at Quebec. They are well known companies of high financial standing. I have the details as to the work the companies are doing at their different places.

To my mind the minister has just given us the most valuable information we have had so far in regard to this item. Assuming that to be correct, one is prompted to inquire, if they are strong companies with large assets, why in the world have they not paid the $25,000 apparently demanded more than once by the government?
It has only been very recently earned and I am not sure that it has not been paid. I am not aware of its having been.
I thought the minister said the practice was to send these accounts out once a month.
That is the practice.

I thought he was dealing with this item and I presumed the account had been rendered. Therefore I wondered, if they are strong companies, why the amount had not been paid.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec

I was only saying it was the practice of the department to render the accounts once a month to any contributing company so that they would know, according to the engineers' estimate, what amount had been earned when they were checking up on the contract. I cannot tell my hon. friend whether or not they have paid. The work is really just well under way. Whether any part of their contribution of 825,000 has been paid,
I am not in a position to say, but I shall be glad to find out.
The minister has already told us, but the information may have been given without consulting the record1. He informed the committee that no portion had been received.
I did not.

Well, we will pass that up.
We ought to know that.
I shall be glad to get the information.

While these are probably substantial companies, this savours in some respects of Belle River. We have a wharf 1,900 feet long. What is the depth of water at the end of it? At Belle River we had to go out further to get five feet of water.

Twenty-five feet at low
water. Since the discussion started I have been informed that they have already paid $18,810.
If we had known that sooner, quite a lot of this discussion might have been avoided.
Who are the contractors? Are they doctors or dentists?
Or lawyers?
The latter would probably be the best. They are Farley & Grant, and Cummins & Robinson, Ottawa.

Item agreed to.
Montebello wharf reconstruction, $10,000.

This is the place where there is to be a large club which is in favour with the Canadian Pacific Railway and which has acquired a territory in and around Montebello for the purpose of developing the fishing and so on. Will the minister give us some of the facts regarding that project? I suppose this wharf is for the purpose of assisting in that development?

It has nothing whatever
to do with that development. It is to reconstruct the landing head 90 feet by 40 feet
in crib work construction from the low water line up, rebuild the wooden approach, raise the whole structure a height of two feet and construct a new two-storey freight shed.

In view of the fact that
there is going to be a sort of summer club at that point, and no doubt many United States visitors are to be invited to go there, might it not be possible to use the dock and freight shed when they are constructed, for storing wet goods?

I shall be glad to make
inquiry and if the facilities can be provided there-

We might go down there
together.
I would even consider that. To be quite serious about the matter, this is for the purpose of repairing an old structure damaged by an ice shove in the spring of 1928.

Is it a wooden
wharf?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Norton creek dredging-the provincial government to contribute a like amount, $3,000.
I notice the amount is very much less than it was last year.

It is just finishing up the
work.

I am glad to hear that. Can the minister undertake that no further money will be inserted in the estimates for the purpose of blasting the bed of this rocky creek in order that it may act as a drain for the surrounding country?

This finishes the work
presently contemplated. I would not like to undertake that this would be the final amount. This is an old story. It started away back in 1912-13, as my hon. friend1 knows, and it has been a bone of contention every once in a while. I quite agree with him that unless these works, as a general rule, can be connected up in some way with some work the Dominion government has done, we should be careful about entering upon them.
Sir GEORGE PERLEY': I know the minister agrees with me that an expenditure for this particular purpose ought not to be undertaken. The Dominion government should not spend money for local drainage purposes. This amount will finish the contract, I understand. The minister says that the government
1944	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
should be very careful about expenditures of this kind. I would go further and say that the government should not spend money for this purpose at all, and I would ask the minister to use his great influence with the government to see that it is not done any more.
After we have been doing it all these years, it is pretty difficult to say that we are going to stop the practice absolutely. Each case must be decided on its merits.
Political merits?

No. This is something
for which the Dominion government, it is claimed, is responsible. That is the main ground of the claim.

Item agreed to.
Norway Bay-wharf reconstruction-to complete, $5,000.
May I ask the minister what has been done and what is required to be done in connection with this work?

This is to complete the
reconstruction of the wharf by rebuilding four cribs in the approach and one crib in the landing head. We spent last year 15,557, and it is estimated that $6,000 will complete the work. The report from the engineer is that part of the landing head of this wharf was built on piles, and considerable damage was done to a portion of the structure by ice. In order to prevent any further damage, a crib will have to be built next year to replace the pilework in the upstream part of the landing head.

Just what use is
made of this wharf?

The engineers report contains this clause:
The above work is required to keep the wharf in a good state of repair for the accommodation of a very large tourist traffic during the summer months. The traffic between Norway Bay and Sand Point over the ferry is fairly heavy. There are two mails daily to and from Sand Point, Ontario, and the structure has to be kept in a safe condition.

This happens to be the only one item in almost three pages of expenditures for the province of Quebec with which I am acquainted. I have heard recently that there is a possibility of this summer resort being flooded by some power project that is under way and is likely to be proceeded with this summer. Has the minister any information on that point?

My information is that
as a result of the work at Chats falls, there will be flooding to some extent at Norway Bay, but, of course, that will have to be compensated for as part of the cost of the Chats falls project.

In view of that, it seems rather strange to be going on with this expenditure. In 1928-29 there was $5,000 in the estimates, in 1929-30, $6,000, and this year an additional $5,000 for a small wharf at a place where there is absolutely no business with the exception of four or five months in the summer, and that only by ferry to Sand Point. If this summer resort is going to be flooded this summer and the wharf made useless, why continue making this expenditure.
If my hon. friend is under the impression that it is only a small wharf, his information is incorrect. It is an extensive wharf about 700 feet long.

The house resumed from March 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woodsworth for the second reading of Bill No. 20, to provide in the province of Ontario for the dissolution and the annulment of marriage, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McMillan.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to say anything about the causes or necessity of divorce, which I know we all aibhor, nor about the principle of divorce and its results, which I know we all deplore. This house has heard many times of its attendant evils, the depraved, or as the case may be, the brokenhearted individual, the broken marriage vows, the broken family circle and the ruined home, and so forth. But rather I want to prove to the house that divorce courts as already established in six of the provinces have increased divorces in Canada because in every case they have facilitated the obtaining of it by a cheaper and easier method.
Before proceeding with the arguments to establish this, may I be pardoned if I make a digression and refer to what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said a few days ago? You will remember he said what we had to deal with was the procedure, not the principle of divorce, that the principle had been settled many years ago. He said we may proceed in one of three ways:
(1)	By action of the federal parliament, as at present or modified;
(2)	By establishing a provincial divorce court, as the bill now before the house proposes;
(3)	By the federal parliament refusing to deal with the petitions.
Mr. Speaker, with all due deference to the Prime Minister, I think there are other ways. One is by the establishment of a court of conciliation and separation, to be presided over by a judge of the supreme court, assisted by one or more experts in social service work. This court, as its name implies, has a dual function. Briefly, its main object would be to effect a reconciliation between husband and wife, thus preserving the unity and sanctity of the home and everything else that that implies. Doubtless this would be quite possible in many cases. Why?
(1)	The sin of adultery, the sole cause of divorce, is no more heinous than many other sins that are forgiven, if not forgotten, by husband or wife, as the case may be.

Divorce Court jor Ontario
(2)	And, in cases where there are children, I venture to say that reconciliation could be and would be effected in almost every case.
(3)	And knowing that separation would preclude remarriage, this would be the strongest incentive to reconciliation.
Failing reconciliation, the court whose establishment I propose would issue a decree of separation, making proper provision for the custody of children, if any, and adequate provision for alimony for the deserving wife.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must not make this digression too long. I may add, however, that this plan would automatically abolish divorce; that is, it would do away with the need for it, as well as prevent remarriage, as remarriage in these cases would constitute bigamy. This scheme could be made to apply to the whole of Canada as well as to Ontario; it would be better, indeed, if applied to the whole of Canada because that would prevent migration from Ontario to other provinces. Doubtless, however, it would drive some people to seek divorce in the American courts, and in the event of a person thus securing divorce, remarrying and establishing a domicile in Canada, he or she could be and should be prosecuted for bigamy. At present I need not elaborate this further, except to say that no one can, be in doubt as to the results of such legislation. Surely we do not want to bring about this state of affairs in Canada, although we seem to be fast approaching it. Last year-1929-there were 816 divorces granted in this country and 1,368 Canadian marriage contracts were annulled by divorce courts in the United States, making altogether 2,184 annulments. Mr. Speaker, I desire to accord the bill now before the house the same support which I gave to a similar measure introduced last year by the same hon. member. The matter has been so thoroughly debated that it seems to me some important points in connection with this legislation have been virtually settled. Particularly is that the case with regard to the question whether or not the adoption of the bill establishing a divorce court would tend in any way to impair the sanctity of the home.
However, there is one thing of which I spoke in discussing the bill last year, which I considered of very great importance and which I have not heard answered either during that debate or during the debate on the bill now under consideration. That is the point that just so long as divorces are granted by the parliament of Canada, just so long shall we be deciding matters of great importance to the people of this country on the most unfair basis possible, that of according justice to people of moderate means or of wealth while absolutely denying it to the poor. I cannot reconcile my conscience to the idea of allowing such a condition as that to continue longer than can be helped.
It has been pointed out, sir, that it is possible for those who desire to obtain decrees of divorce to go before the Senate committee and obtain a remission of the usual fees in order that they may not be put to expense which they can ill afford. As a citizen of this country I resent the suggestion that any man or woman should be called upon to proclaim his or her poverty in order to obtain justice. So far as I am aware there is no regularly constituted court of justice in any province where a citizen is told at the outset, "Because you are poor you need not come to this court looking for justice on any claim which you may have to present." There is

Divorce Court for Ontario
not a man in this house familiar with the procedure in courts of justice in Canada but knows perfectly well that the poor man or woman who comes before our regularly constituted courts of justice can do so without being put in the position of paying fees which he or she can ill afford. No lawyer of standing whom I know or with whom I have come in contact will refuse to take a case which represents itself to him as being just. In fact, the members of the Ontario bar-and I presume the same condition applies in the other provinces-take an oath when they are admitted to practice that they will refuse no just cause. However, a lawyer who is approached in connection with a divorce case by a man or a woman of small or very moderate means has to ask the preliminary question, before he even considers the justice or injustice of the cause: " Have you so much money, not for me, but for the parliament of Canada, which demands so much before you can hope to get any justice regardless of what your evidence may be?" I challenge truthful denial of the statement that the result of this condition has been that anyone who comes to a lawyer with a divorce case must state, as a preliminary, that he or she has upwards of $1,000 to put down in order to obtain that justice.
Surely, sir, that condition reflects most shamefully upon our laws and regulations with regard to the administration of justice. It was said only a few moments ago, by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, that the establishment of these courts would largely increase the number of divorces, and my hon. friend quoted figures, as he is entitled to do and which figures are deserving of some consideration, in an endeavour to show the house that if these courts were established such would be the case. But, sir, no consideration of these figures or of any figures which can be brought forward has any value unless we are able to include in them the number of persons, which reasonable and moderate estimates place at from 1,200 to 1,500 annually, who go across the line to get the justice which is denied them in this Dominion of Canada. That again, sir, is something which reflects upon us in a way that does this Dominion and its administration of justice no credit.
The number of divorces granted by parliament has increased also.
And the number of divorces here has increased, as my hon. friend points out.
May I ask a question? Could you not achieve your end just as well if the fees were reduced by this parliament?

The obvious answer to that question, I think, is that there has been no suggestion made and no disposition shown, so far as I have ever heard, to reduce the fees. Those who are opposing this bill are not suggesting, so far as I have been able to gather, an alternative measure looking to the reduction of the cost; they simply say the bill should be defeated absolutely. I am very glad my hon. friend, with his usual fairness, brought up that question, because it draws attention once more to another aspect of the situation which in my view is most important. Under the procedure of the only divorce tribunal which we have, the Senate of Canada, all such cases must be brought to Ottawa. That in itself makes the whole thing prohibitive to people of small means or people who are poor. In connection with no other court of justice or any other judicial tribunal is it necessary to journey to the capital of the nation, together with all witnesses, paying railway fares, hotel bills and the hundred and one other incidentals which so vastly increase the cost of the application which is presented. If it were necessary or imperative that a man having a claim to present before a court of justice should bring that claim to Ottawa and transport all his witnesses to Ottawa, what a cry would go out! The people would say, "You are making justice in this country prohibitive; establish courts in every province so that the poor man may have an opportunity of reaching them with the convenience offered to the rich." Apart altogether from the cost of the divorce legislation under the present system, apart altogether from the cost of the necessary agency work which has to be done, we have this almost unsurmountable obstacle presented in a great number of cases, in that witnesses must be brought to Ottawa and the expenses incident to that procedure are piled upon the applicant. If he has not the money to afford taking that course, what does he do? He crosses the Detroit river and goes into the state of Michigan or some other adjacent state in order to get his decree.
During the course of this debate some hon. gentlemen have said that the province of Ontario has not asked for this bill. I dare say that it is now within the knowledge of all hon. gentlemen that the premier of Ontario has specifically pointed out that it does not lie upon that province to ask for legislation from this parliament, but that on the contrary it is the obligation of every hon. member of this house, whether from the province of Ontario or otherwise, to take upon himself the responsibility of dealing with this question. Mr. Speaker, looking at it from that viewpoint, looking at it from the viewpoint of

one who wants to see every man who has just cause receive justice in this matter, as in all other matters where a person appears before any judicial forum as a seeker after justice, I ask this house to pass this bill and do away with the inequality which has become, in my humble opinion, a disgrace to Canada.

It is an act of parliament and they have a right to do that. And we know, it is done; but no judge would ever allow anyone to discuss with him a question that came before his court. Before the Senate committee there are no recorded decisions, no precedents set up, as in a court, for the presiding officer to be guided by. In ordinary cases, in every court, there are reports, decisions, to guide the judges in dealing with cases which come before them, but in the high court of parliament a chairman in one committee may be giving a decision to-day and at the same time another chairman in another part of the building may be giving a diametrically opposite decision. If these cases were heard before a court, the people asking for relief, would have a right, should the court find against their plea, to go before another court and appeal. That is not possible in this case. This is an act of parliament; it is a statute once it is passed and there is no appeal.
As regards divorce cases, there are no set decisions, no set rules. Divorce may be granted through the houses of parliament for any cause whatsoever that the chairman of the divorce committee happens to think fit. There are no definite rules set up. It does not have to be any one thing or another. The chairman makes his own ruling and a bill of this parliament is passed.
The question of publicity is very important. In a province which has a divorce court there is no publicity to the proceedings. You never see in our papers any report of a divorce case; only the decisions are given. But in parliament some 400 copies of the evidence are printed and distributed. Every member of the house, every senator receives a copy. These are broadcast and the evidence is placed in concrete form so that any person, even a child, may read it.

When the hon. gentleman speaks of this evidence as being broadcast as printed literature, is he speaking only for himself? He is not speaking for me; I have never broadcast such literature. Let him speak for himself.

I was not speaking of the hon. gentleman or of any other hon. member. I was simply saying that some 400 copies of the evidence taken in every divorce case are printed and distributed to at least some 400 people. They are in print to be brought up at some future time and thrown in the face of some child. That is entirely unnecessary In a divorce court the evidence is not made public in any form.
Under our present system of granting divorce, one, two or three parties may be named as respondents. They may not appear at all. They may be entirely innocent. There is no written decision of the chairman of the divorce committee exonerating them from blame or finding them innocent. Any evidence that may be given-and they may not be present to defend themselves and may not be represented by anyone to defend them-goes out in the printed record. This evidence is never refuted, and the chairman of the divorce committee does not give a decision holding them blameless in such a case. Thus other innocent people may be damaged by the present system of divorce as granted by parliament. In the divorce courts in the provinces which have such courts, there is, I believe, a representative of the crown who, acting as king's proctor, looks especially for collusion and may defend any respondent who does not happen to be present. In that way a fairer trial is secured and there is less chance of

Item agreed to.
Port Stanley-harbour repairs and improvements, $150,000.

Before we adjourned at six o'clock the minister and the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) were explaining some points in connection with this item.
I wanted to ask the minister as to the amount of business passing through this port, and particularly whether Port Stanley was one of the places which had one of the liquor export docks.
No, we were just asking for information.

I am sure if hon. members opposite understood the merits of this item they would not question the expenditure. Port Stanley is situated at just about the centre of the north shore of lake Erie, and serves as the distributing centre for a large
[111-. Elliott.]
part of western Ontario. The chief business there is the bringing in of bulk coal; the bringing in of coal by the ferry company and the bringing in of tourists on the daily boats which ply between Cleveland and Port Stanley. There is also the fishing industry, and the Canada Steamship Linas make Port Stanley a port of call.
I do not want to take the time of the committee in quoting a 'lot of figures, but I might just show how the business has increased. With regard to bulk coal, 17,000 tons were brought in during 1925, while in 1929 that increased to 177,000 tons. In 1925 the ferry *company brought in 174,000 tons of coal, while in 1929 they brought in 251,000 tons. The total merchandise brought into Part Stanley in 1925 amounted t.o 191,000 tons, and in 1929 that figure increased to 428,000 tons. Had there been increased facilities there for warehouses, according to the engineer's report business would have been much greater. Port Stanley is also a celebrated summer resort, with a line of steamships running to Cleveland. In 1926 there were 14,900 passengers brought to Port Stanley on these boats, and that number increased in 1928 to over 20,000 passengers; in fact during 1928 and 1929 approximately 40,000 'passengers came from Cleveland; 'bringing with them 6,258 automobiles. While we cannot get any accurate estimate, I would judge that these people during the two years spent dlose to $800,000 in that vicinity. The amount of customs duties collected there has increased from $19,000 in 1925 to $107,000 in 1929, and that in itself represents only a smalll portion of the dutiable goods Which passed through that port, because we must remember that the 251,000 tons of bituminous coal, a large portion of which was dutiable, was consigned to other ports. In fact, goods are manifested through Port Stanley for 98 inland ports. Practically all this trade is carried over the London and Port Stanley railway which is owned by the city of London. This is a very good source of revenue for that railway as otherwise there would 'be a larger deficit which would have to be made up by direct taxation on the people of London. This port not only serves t'he county of Elgin but, as I have said, is the distributing centre for practically the entire southern peninsula. I am sure my hon. friend from Hamilton will not object to this vote, because at the present time the coking plant in that city brings in a great deal, if not all, of its coal through Port Stanley. This coal travels to London over the London and Port Stanley railway and then goes to Hamilton over the Canadian National.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Ontario
I think that is all I need say, unless my hon. friends desire further information. I might add that in southern Ontario the people appreciate very much the facilities which are being provided for the increased business there by the Department of Public Works, and I am sure if my hon. friend from Pictou understood the situation he would not object to this item.
There was no export dock there?
No, but on perhaps four or five occasions liquor was shipped out of Port Stanley directly from freight cars into a rum running boat. There was no licensed liquor export dock there.

I fully realize the importance
of Port Stanley. Just before six o'clock I was asking the minister whether the department had received any assurance that a coking plant was to be established at that place. Up until last year the facilities were quite adequate to accommodate all the traffic at Port Stanley; I think there can be no doubt of that. Is it not a fact that the new facilities at Port Stanley were to be the deciding factor as to whether that coking plant should be established there or whether it would go to another port on lake Erie, Port Maitland, which has facilities which are perfectly adequate? From what I understand of the situation it seems that if these facilities were not established at Port Stanley possibly the coking plant would not have gone there. Has any assurance been given to the department that a coking plant will be established there if the facilities are increased?

The department has not
taken sides as between Port Stanley and Port Maitland or any other port; we are only trying to provide for the business which comes to these ports or which is in prospect through the efforts put forth by the people in the vicinity. We do not take sides as between these different ports. There is no definite assurance with regard to the coking plant, although there is a fairly definite assurance that they expect to locate there. There is nothing binding them as far as the department is concerned, and there is nothing binding the department to provide any facilities for them. Every new industry which proposes to locate anywhere receives very sympathetic consideration at the hands of the department. If Port Maitland or any other port has an industry in prospect, nothing is done by the department or any of the officials to divert that industry to any other port.

I am sure, the explanation of
the minister is satisfactory as far as it goes. He told us before six o'clock that these facilities probably would be needed, but I do not think there has been any damage to the facilities which were there previously; the piers are not particularly out of repair. Will the additional facilities to be provided by this vote of $150,000, together with the $50,000 spent last year, be sufficient if a coking plant is established at Port Stanley?

No, these facilities are just for the present needs at that point. If a coking plant is established there, further substantial expenditures will be necessary; and from all the information we have we believe more business is expected. My hon. friend has been told of the increase in business at Port Stanley in recent years, and I am told that the only reason that increase has not been greater is that the facilities would not take care of any further increase.

I think the hon. minister will
agree with me that the same increase in business would apply to the other ports on that great lake.
I am delighted to say that that is correct; all those ports are doing very well.

I am sorry to have to say that most of the goods are coming into the country rather than being exported. I think the member for West Elgin made the statement that most of the coal coming into that port goes to Hamilton, and that practically all the supplies for the coking plant at Hamilton come through Port Stanley. I am afraid he is misinformed in regard to that, because a considerable amount of traffic comes through Port Maitland to go over the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway, not only for Hamilton but for other points. I do not wish to press this matter further, but it seems to me that we should be very careful about these expenditures.

I thing I mentioned to the minister some years ago and even last year that the Bow river at the city of Calgary had its course diverted considerably for two reasons: first, on account of the government giving a company the right to put a dam across the river, throwing the whole course of the river against the government's own boulevard. In the second place the government took no care to protect its own boulevard and because of that, the river washed into the city and washed a large part of its property away. The city endeavoured to fill in between the groins with stone. The Department of Public Works or the irrigation department for a time even endeavoured to stop the city from filling in between the groins, because it was represented to them they would be throwing the river back on its old course. The minister no doubt received a recommendation from a joint committee of citizens representing the New Westminster board of trade, the mayor and city council, the harbour commissioners and officials of Pacific Coast Terminals Limited in October of last year.
Yes, I remember that.

He has been told of the increase there has been in the shipping at that port from 1921, when we had only thirteen vessels and a net tonnage of 38,987 tons, to 1929, when we had 198 ships with a net tonnage' of 625,271 tons. The representation of the joint committee was that there was difficulty experienced by shippers in that they required to have a minimum depth of thirty feet on a twelve foot tide. They have had instances recently of three or four lines of deep sea vessels that refused to come up the river, claiming that there was not sufficient depth. The minister, I have no doubt, is familiar with these facts. It is absolutely necessary to have a minimum draft of thirty feet. That is the objective set by the citizens of New Westminster and other points along the river, and the figure at which they have been aiming for a great many years. In the recommendation of that joint committee certain requirements were pointed out. The first was for the construction of 8,000 feet of the south jetty during the fiscal year 1930-31; the second was that the north jetty be continued to deep water; the third, that the Annieville training wall be extended downstream the necessary distance in order to eliminate the Annieville bar; and the fourth, that permanent construction be undertaken on the Sapperton bar so as to create a permanent channel of 700 to 800 feet on each side thereof. The first item, I understand, has been accepted by the minister.

The government has perhaps been working on it; no doubt the chief engineer and the deputy minister are interested, but at the same time we want results. IV e want to get ships in that are waiting to come into that port; as the minister knows, the port of New Westminster is becoming one of the great ports of Canada. There is no doubt that in a comparatively short time the Fraser river will be the industrial centre of the mainland of British Columbia. I know that the minister's colleague who sits to his left, the former incumbent of the office, is very much interested in the port of New Westminster, and he knows that what I am saying is perfectly correct. There is also another matter which came uip for consideration just last winter, with regard to the ice in the river particularly above the Fraser river bridge. We had an unusually cold spell this year, and it looked as though there might be trouble both below and above the bridge. A channel was kept open below the bridge through the efforts [Mr. Elliott.J
of this department, but the large industries which are situated above the bridge had to close down, adding greatly to the unemployment which prevailed this year. It seems to me it would have been comparatively easy to have kept the river clear of ice both above and below the bridge, or at least to have kept a channel open. The suggestion I should like to make to the minister is that he and his officials consider the advisability of converting the dredge 303 into an ice breaker. I think that could be done at very little cost, simply by putting some sheets of steel on the bow. As the minister knows, this is a suction dredge and it could take enough water into its hold to give it the necessary weight. It has the power, and if the bow were reinforced with steel, which could be done at trifling expense, there would be no question as to her ability to keep the channel of the Fraser river open regardless of what kind of weather prevailed. The ice in that river comes from up above; as the minister knows, the river is several hundred miles long and the ice comes down from up above and causes this blockade at the bridge.
My suggestion to the minister is that the 303 is not very much good anyway for any other purpose; I am sure the deputy minister will not agree with me. The boat may be useful for some work on the river there, but as a general utility dredge it does not compare at all with the King Edward. I have said this before, but I am afraid my remarks have not had much effect. I think the 303 should be junked; it is an old dredge which was brought over from Germany, I believe twenty-five or thirty years ago, and it is out of date. I do not suggest, of course, that there should not be a second dredge on the Fraser river, but I suggest that there should be a new dredge of the King Edward type constructed, and I think a lot of money would be saved if that were done. I have discussed this matter several times with the deputy minister, but he considers the results achieved by the 303 quite satisfactory. I do not believe that is so, I think it would be a good idea if we could get rid of that 303 except for use as an ice breaker or for work for which she is suitable. All she does is dig holes; she cannot construct a channel and never has been able to do so. All the channel work has been gone over by the King Edward after the 303 finished. The 303 simply digs holes and never finishes a job. I wish the minister would take up that matter with his officials and see whether it would not be good business to give us a new, modern dredge of the King Edward type on the Fraser river.
